class.name: PXTGI3D
class.experimental: Its look, settings and cost may still change.
class.brief_description: Real-time global illumination traced against the physics shapes (PXTGI), provided by the PhysX module.
class.description: Adds bounce light to the whole scene, every frame, with nothing to bake: light from the sun, [OmniLight3D]s, [SpotLight3D]s and emissive surfaces bounces off what it reaches and colours what is around it, and moving objects take part as they move. Add one node to a scene; where it sits does not matter. Each visible surface sends rays out. A ray first follows what is on screen; where it leaves the screen or passes behind what the screen shows, it continues against the scene's collision shapes ([CollisionShape3D]s of every physics body, static ones included), which stand in for the geometry. So walls, floors and objects only bounce light off-screen if they have collision shapes; a body's colour is taken from its [MeshInstance3D]'s material. A hidden collision shape (it, its body or a parent not visible) is left out, as is a disabled one: hiding a shape takes it out of the GI without changing its collision, for example a player's capsule that has no mesh of its own. [Area3D] shapes are trigger volumes and take no part. Emissive meshes without a body still give off light, as their bounding box (not those whose [member GeometryInstance3D.gi_mode] is Disabled, which Godot's own GI leaves out too). A ray of the radiance cache that leaves the scene sees the sky (or the background colour), so surfaces that see out get the sky's light and closed spaces don't. A body's look comes from the [MeshInstance3D] under it, or else the one it sits under (a model with its collision body as a child), or else the first one beside it (in a node of up to 8 children, such as a model holding its mesh and its body): its albedo from the first surface with a [BaseMaterial3D], its glow from its brightest surface. PXTGI can't read a [ShaderMaterial]: give one a [code]pxtgi_albedo[/code] and/or [code]pxtgi_emission[/code] [Color] in its metadata (set with [method Object.set_meta]), or a [code]pxtgi_emission[/code] Color on the [MeshInstance3D] for the whole mesh, or either on the physics body itself; otherwise it bounces as neutral grey and gives off no light off screen. Lights: the sun is the brightest visible [DirectionalLight3D] that lights surfaces (not one in [constant DirectionalLight3D.SKY_MODE_SKY_ONLY]); of the [OmniLight3D]s and [SpotLight3D]s, the 8 of each that Godot draws whose reach comes nearest the camera, chosen every frame (faded out as Godot fades them with distance fade on). Lights, shapes and meshes added to or removed from the scene are picked up within a few frames, without walking the whole scene. With [member ProjectSettings.rendering/lights_and_shadows/use_physical_light_units] on, lights and emission are taken at the strength Godot renders them (their intensity in lumens, lux or nits, and the camera's exposure). The result is also used for reflections on smooth surfaces (see [member reflection_mode]). Works with the Forward+ renderer only. It uses SDFGI as its switch: while the node is visible it turns on SDFGI in the scene's [Environment] at its cheapest settings (one cascade) and replaces SDFGI's light with its own; hidden or removed, the environment's own SDFGI settings are back. The scene needs an [Environment] (a [WorldEnvironment] or the camera's). Hiding the node turns it off, as with a light: Godot's own lighting is back until it is shown again. Every viewport of the world (a minimap, a camera feed, split screen) keeps its own history. While a PXTGI3D is visible, Godot's SDFGI step is replaced everywhere, so another [World3D] can't use SDFGI at the same time (VoxelGI alone is unaffected). [b]Reflection probes override PXTGI inside their box[/b], as they do Godot's SDFGI and VoxelGI: a [ReflectionProbe] with an [member ReflectionProbe.intensity] above 0 replaces PXTGI's traced reflections with its cubemap, and one whose [member ReflectionProbe.ambient_mode] isn't [constant ReflectionProbe.AMBIENT_DISABLED] replaces its bounce light with the probe's ambient. PXTGI doesn't trace what such a probe replaces (inside its box, less its [member ReflectionProbe.blend_distance], for probes whose [member ReflectionProbe.reflection_mask] covers every layer), so a probe-lit area costs little. A probe with its ambient mode Disabled keeps PXTGI's bounce light and only supplies the reflections; one with an intensity of 0 keeps PXTGI's traced reflections.

members.member: Shows one stage of the work instead of the lit scene, to see what each adds. [code]0[/code] is off (the normal result).
How strong the bounce light is: [code]1.0[/code] is physically based; higher brightens it artistically.
How far, in metres, rays follow what is on screen before continuing against the collision shapes.

If [code]true[/code], light bounces more than once: surfaces lit by bounce light pass some of it on, filling dark corners and enclosed spaces. If [code]false[/code], one bounce only, which is darker. It is usually no cheaper: with it on, the light at off-screen surfaces is kept in a radiance cache and refreshed a little each frame; with it off, every ray that leaves the screen lights what it hits from scratch, with a shadow ray to the sun and to every omni and spot light. The more lights, the more leaving it on saves (about half the cost in a level with many lights); only with few lights and a lot of moving clutter (a collapsing pile) is turning it off slightly cheaper.

Rays each traced point sends per frame, from [code]1[/code] to [code]4[/code]. More rays settle faster and flicker less when the camera or the lights move, at about proportional cost. [code]2[/code] suits most daylight scenes; scenes lit mostly by emissives or small lights (night) look steadier with [code]4[/code].

Reflections on surfaces smoother than [member reflection_roughness_cutoff]: [code]0[/code] leaves them to Godot (reflection probes, sky, screen-space reflection); [code]1[/code] traces them on screen; [code]2[/code] traces them on screen, then against the collision shapes, so what is behind the camera or off screen is reflected too; [code]3[/code] (Traced + Probes) also uses the [ReflectionProbe]s with an intensity of 0 (see below), costing a texture read per reflective pixel inside them. Inside a probe's box the probe's cubemap replaces the traced reflections (as it does SDFGI's), whatever this is set to: give a probe an intensity of 0 to keep the traced reflections inside it (its ambient light, if any, still applies). With Traced + Probes, inside the box of a probe with an intensity of 0, PXTGI draws the probe's reflection itself: below the roughness cutoff the reflections are traced, and what is off screen takes its colour from the probe's capture where the probe could see it (on static bodies only: textures and detail the collision shapes don't have); rays that find nothing, the fade below the cutoff, and rougher surfaces get the probe's own reflection (box projected if the probe is) instead of the sky. The probe is still captured by Godot as usual: with [member ReflectionProbe.update_mode] Once that happens once, and its lighting stays as it was then. Turn on the probe's [member ReflectionProbe.enable_shadows]: without it the capture has no shadows, and what lies in shadow is reflected as if lit.

Surfaces below this roughness get traced reflections ([member reflection_mode]); rougher ones keep Godot's own reflection (reflection probes, sky). The traced reflection fades into Godot's over the last quarter of the cutoff (from [code]0.375[/code] to [code]0.5[/code] at the default), so materials on either side of it don't look abruptly different. Traced reflections cost per pixel, so a cutoff that includes many common materials costs a lot: at [code]0.5[/code], glossy and mirror-like surfaces are traced, while the broad, blurry reflections of rougher surfaces look the same from a probe.

How far, in metres, rays go against the collision shapes. Shorter is cheaper in large, cluttered scenes, but light from surfaces further than this is not bounced (it falls back to the environment's ambient light). Indoor scenes may look darker if this is shorter than the room.
